See al-Kindī’s Treatise on First Philosophy (same source, vol. 1, pp. 118–119). In al-Kindī’s terminology, tahawwī means the realization of a thing’s identity—that is, its coming into existence. Ays means existence, while lays here means non-existence. In al-Jurjānī’s Definitions, “identity” is explained as an expression for the absolute reality that contains all realities as a seed contains the tree, arising from the absolute unseen. Al-Kindī’s phrase therefore means that the thing came into existence from non-existence.↩︎

The phrase “the counting of the duration of what changes” means that motion measures the time of a changing thing. The Arabic word used here is an active participle from the verb “to count,” meaning to calculate or enumerate.↩︎

A thing’s inniyya means its reality or true nature. The word is formed from inna, the particle used at the beginning of a declarative sentence to affirm the reality of something. Inniyya is an abstract noun formed in the same way as “humanity” from “human” or “existentiality” from “existence.”↩︎

Aristotle defines the soul as “the first actuality of a natural, organized body capable of life” (2, 412b 5). In Aristotle, form plays the role of actuality—or completion—in relation to matter, which remains only potentially existent until form brings its existence into actuality (Aristotle, 12, 1069b 34). Richard Walzer supports our view that when al-Kindī speaks of the soul as “form,” he means the term in Aristotle’s sense. Walzer says that al-Kindī “refers to Aristotle’s definition of the soul as the form of the body or the completion of the body” (Walzer, Islamic Philosophy and Its Place in Human Thought, trans. Tawfīq Ḥusayn, p. 41).↩︎

This conclusion is confirmed by another passage from al-Kindī himself, in his treatise on “the prostration of the outermost body” (Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 247), where he says: “Form is not separate from its element; the two are united....”↩︎
